extracted.intended_audience: public relations students and practitioners; internal communication managers
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluation criteria for designing and assessing employee/member communication programs within organizations and associations, including audience segmentation, content strategy, and five concrete evaluation methods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Internal-External Communication Objective
rubrics_metrics.description: Internal communication programs are extremely important because employees communicate information about the organization to external publics; failing to meet internal objectives can make it difficult to meet external objectives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design internal programs so employees are well informed and feel positively about the organization; recognize that employees who dislike or are poorly informed about the organization will communicate those attitudes to outsiders.

rubrics_metrics.name: Member Relations in Associations — two-way symmetric communication
rubrics_metrics.description: Associations tend to be less-structured organizations whose member-communication program must consist of two-way symmetric communication, designed to get the appropriate information to members when they need it and to facilitate communication among members.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because members are autonomous and join for essential information (products, regulations, research), associations should prioritize open, specialized horizontal channels and mechanisms for member-to-member exchange.

rubrics_metrics.name: Segment internal publics by Grunig's situational theory dimensions
rubrics_metrics.description: Translate Grunig’s situational theory into internal-public terms: employees differ in problem recognition, perceived constraints, and perceived involvement, and each employee public requires a different communication strategy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess employees on: (1) what problems/tasks they face (information relevance), (2) their level of autonomy/constraints, and (3) their involvement. Use these measures to tailor channels, messages, and interactivity levels.

rubrics_metrics.name: Management can create internal publics via task/constraint/involvement changes
rubrics_metrics.description: Because the management subsystem can change tasks, constraints, and involvement, it has the power to create different kinds of employee publics—something that cannot be done with external publics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that organizational design choices (centralization, job design, decision authority) will change communication needs and can be used strategically to produce desired public types.

rubrics_metrics.name: Match communication strategy to organizational structure
rubrics_metrics.description: Highly structured organizations will have many low-involvement, constrained or fatalistic publics lower in the hierarchy and a few high-involvement publics at the top; less-structured organizations will have high-involvement problem-facing publics dispersed throughout.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In structured organizations, prioritize downward accurate transmission (management-to-subordinates) and human-relations-style media for lower-level employees; in less-structured organizations, facilitate horizontal/crisscross interpersonal communication and subsystem-specific channels.

rubrics_metrics.name: Differentiate content for specialist vs lower-level publics
rubrics_metrics.description: Employee publications serve two purposes: for specialists, they integrate by making specialists aware of other specialists' work (research features, policy, budgets); some lower-level service workers will process the same information but also need human-relations information (pay, benefits, social activities) to gain pseudo-involvement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design publications with diversified content: place current organizational news up front, include research/features for specialists, and employee profiles/achievements/social activity pieces for lower-level workers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Employee publications should be diversified in less-structured organizations
rubrics_metrics.description: In nonstructured organizations, employee publications must be diversified—like commercial media—containing current organizational news up front, research features, employee profiles, and articles about employee achievements and social activities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use a mix of hard news and feature content to serve specialists (who will process research info) and lower-level employees (who seek human-relations material).

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate Communication by exposure, retention, and acceptance
rubrics_metrics.description: Internal communication (particularly downward) can be evaluated by determining exposure to publications/sources, whether employees retain and believe messages, and by asking specific questions to measure these outcomes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: measure distribution timeliness (e.g., 'received within 48 hours'), retention (do employees remember reading specific stories), readability (written at appropriate level), and acceptance (understandable, presents both sides, seen as an excellent source). Appropriate for structured organizations and to test message flow in less-structured ones.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coorientational evaluations (mutual perceptions and agreement)
rubrics_metrics.description: The coorientation method measures how accurately two groups (e.g., superiors and subordinates) predict the cognitions and attitudes of the other, and the extent of their understanding and agreement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use to detect mismatches (e.g., nonmanagement underestimating management concerns, management underestimating employee concerns). In unstructured organizations, use to measure cross-subsystem prediction accuracy essential for coordination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Human Relations Audits (attitudes toward job/supervisor/organization)
rubrics_metrics.description: Human relations audits use questionnaires to measure employee attitudes toward their job, supervisor, and the organization; they indicate whether human relations techniques have affected attitudes and behavior.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Useful primarily for evaluating impression/attitude-focused objectives in structured organizations; do not substitute for measures of message retention or acceptance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Communication Satisfaction (ICA audit) — measure perceived communication effectiveness
rubrics_metrics.description: The ICA communication-audit questionnaire asks employees how much information they receive and whether they need more on topics (job duties, pay/benefits, performance); it asks about communication with superiors/subordinates/coworkers, channels used, and outcomes such as job satisfaction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The audit captures perceptions and specific experiences of effective/ineffective communication. Limitations: it measures perceived satisfaction (often confounded with overall job satisfaction) and thus may not reflect objective communication effectiveness — supplement with objective measures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Network analysis — who talks to whom and how messages flow
rubrics_metrics.description: A network analysis develops diagrams of who talks to whom and how messages flow, and can measure retention by comparing what people say they heard with an original message released into the organization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Especially useful for unstructured organizations (unscheduled communication). Five kinds: duty study (self-recording), observers (trained observers record interactions), cross-sectional interview/questionnaire, 'small-world' technique (release and trace a message), and diffusion/ECCO method (trace naturally occurring messages). Use network analysis to learn unscheduled flows and effectiveness of informal networks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose evaluation technique according to organizational structure and communication goals
rubrics_metrics.description: Which evaluation technique should be used depends on the structure of the organization and the relevant goals and objectives of its communication system.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Structured orgs: use exposure/retention/acceptance measures, human relations audits; Unstructured orgs: use coorientation, network analysis, and methods that reveal horizontal/crisscross flows.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measure and address accuracy of upward communication from lower levels
rubrics_metrics.description: Research suggests that in highly structured organizations, upward communication from lower-to-higher-level employees usually will be distorted in favor of what the superior wants to hear; lower-level employees also tend to process rather than seek information from outsiders.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To get accurate external information, organizations should use formal polls or formal communication channels; appoint administrators who interact with or are similar to clients to improve accuracy of incoming information.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess employees' external communication behavior
rubrics_metrics.description: Employees who are most active/ involved internally (management and more-educated younger publics) also communicate most to outsiders; employees who face high constraints and low involvement have little reason to talk about the organization outside.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use surveys of employee external communication frequency/contents to understand which internal publics act as organizational ambassadors and to shape internal messaging accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use objective measures to complement satisfaction/perception audits
rubrics_metrics.description: Satisfaction and human-relations audits measure perceptions and attitudes, which can be biased by overall job satisfaction; therefore, objective measures (e.g., message retention tests, distribution timing checks, readability scores) are necessary to evaluate actual communication effectiveness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Combine subjective (ICA audit, human relations audit) and objective (distribution timing, readability, recall tests, network traces) to get a fuller picture of internal communication performance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design employee media to match publics' media use patterns
rubrics_metrics.description: Different employee publics use different media: management uses employee publications for hard news; older employees prefer soft human-relations material; specialists rely more on interpersonal/technical channels; nonspecialists use media for employee-context items.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Segment content and channels: provide hard news/policy for management; features and human-interest pieces for older/low-involvement employees; technical journals/seminars and interpersonal facilitation for specialists.

rubrics_metrics.name: Network-analysis retention check (message diffusion vs recall)
rubrics_metrics.description: Some network-analysis techniques measure retention of messages by asking people what they have heard and comparing what they say with an original message released into the organization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this to quantify distortion, selective processing, and the fidelity of information transmitted through informal networks; select 'small-world' or diffusion/ECCO methods depending on whether messages are injected or naturally occurring.
